name: Djent
about: Djent is named for the onomatopoeia of its signature sound: a palm-muted, compressed chord on an eight-string guitar, played in syncopated polyrhythms against a straight drum pulse. The vocabulary belongs to Meshuggah, who had refined it on Nothing and obZen before a generation of bedroom guitarists, led by Periphery's Misha Mansoor, turned it into a style around 2008 through forum demos and YouTube playthroughs. Britain's Sikth and the Netherlands' Textures supplied the earlier template; TesseracT added atmosphere and clean singing, Animals as Leaders instrumental virtuosity, Vildhjarta pure dissonance. Its production is clinical, its rhythms mathematical, and its melodies, when they come, owe more to pop and fusion than to metal. By the mid-2010s it had been absorbed into progressive metal and metalcore, with Northlane and Spiritbox carrying it to arenas.

artists.name: Meshuggah
artists.why: the source of the entire vocabulary

artists.name: Periphery
artists.why: Misha Mansoor's band named the scene

artists.name: Textures
artists.why: Dutch pioneers of the polyrhythmic groove

artists.name: Monuments
artists.why: London technicians with a soulful singer

artists.name: Northlane

albums.title: obZen
albums.why: Bleed's relentless kick-drum pattern became the genre's exam piece, and the album around it is Meshuggah at their most concise and brutal.

albums.title: Nothing
albums.why: The band's first album on eight-string guitars, slower and heavier than anything before it, and the tonal blueprint every djent band chased.

albums.title: The Trees Are Dead & Dried Out Wait for Something Wild
albums.why: Two vocalists, hyperactive tapping riffs and a prankish streak, the British band's debut was years ahead of the scene it later inspired.

albums.title: Drawing Circles
albums.why: The Dutch band's second album balanced Meshuggah-style grooves with soaring clean choruses, a template later bands made standard.

albums.title: The Hidden Words
albums.why: A short-lived Milton Keynes band whose only album seeded both Monuments and TesseracT, and whose riffs still sound of the moment.

albums.title: Rareform
albums.why: Eight-string grooves meet deathcore breakdowns on the Minneapolis band's second album, an early American bridge between the two styles.

albums.title: Animals as Leaders
albums.why: Tosin Abasi's instrumental debut, produced by Misha Mansoor, showed the eight-string guitar could carry melody, fusion harmony and groove without a voice.

albums.title: Periphery
albums.why: Years of forum demos finally collected on a debut that gave the scene its name, its production standard and a pop sensibility in Spencer Sotelo's vocals.

albums.title: At the Dream's Edge
albums.why: Paul Ortiz's one-man instrumental project is djent at its most melodic and synth-coated, a bedroom-studio record that holds up.

albums.title: Beacons
albums.why: Ben Sharp's self-released instrumental album, built on cockpit voice-recorder transcripts, is the scene's great DIY cult record.

albums.title: One
albums.why: The Concealing Fate suite and Daniel Tompkins's clean, reverbed vocals gave djent an atmospheric, almost progressive-rock dimension.

albums.title: Måsstaden
albums.why: The Swedes' debut is the darkest record in the style: dissonant, downtuned and eerie, with a cold ambience its many imitators rarely match.

albums.title: Februus
albums.why: A long, immersive French debut that wrapped crushing low-end grooves in ambient passages and Matthieu Romarin's elastic vocals.

albums.title: Via
albums.why: Los Angeles groove with a hip-hop bounce and two vocalists, the point where djent met the American hardcore crowd.

albums.title: The Discovery
albums.why: Synth-heavy, technical deathcore from Chicago whose polyrhythmic riffing made it a fixture on djent lists.

albums.title: Periphery II: This Time It's Personal
albums.why: Bigger choruses, guest solos and sharper songwriting made the second album the band's most complete statement.

albums.title: Gnosis
albums.why: John Browne's riffs and Matt Rose's soulful singing produce a tight, groove-led debut that stands apart from the scene's clinical tendencies.

albums.title: Altered State
albums.why: A continuous concept album with saxophone and Ashe O'Hara's vocals, the band's most melodic and progressive record.

albums.title: The Joy of Motion
albums.why: The trio's third album brought in jazz, flamenco and electronic textures, loosening the mathematics into genuinely musical writing.

albums.title: Language
albums.why: Michael Lessard's arrival turned the Indianapolis band from deathcore into airy, Cynic-indebted progressive metal with djent rhythms underneath.

albums.title: Handmade Cities
albums.why: Warm, melodic instrumental guitar from Sydney that stripped the style of its aggression and kept the rhythmic intelligence.

albums.title: Meta
albums.why: Long Island mathcore veterans borrowing djent's low-end precision for a record of whiplash tempo changes and unexpected melody.

albums.title: Alien
albums.why: Marcus Bridge's personal lyrics and a heavy dose of industrial electronics pushed the Australians' djent-metalcore into darker, more popular territory.

albums.title: Eternal Blue
albums.why: Courtney LaPlante's range, from pop melody to screams, over polished djent grooves made the Canadian band's debut the style's biggest crossover in years.
